doc.title: Tom Scott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Alto and tenor, and Cannonball, Miles and Coltrane
summary: Scott prefers alto for jazz and contrasts Miles, Coltrane and Cannonball.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: Which is your favorite — I’ll rephrase. Do you think of yourself as a saxophone player as my alto is more of my jazz horn, my tenor is more of my pop horn? Is that not relevant?

It’s a good question. I think in my mind — I mean look I play pop music on alto and tenor and jazz on alto and tenor. I think if you were to ask me to pick the instrument that I feel most comfortable about playing jazz on it’s probably the alto. And of course Cannonball Adderley especially has been an incredible influence on my playing and continues to be to this day. Oh look at him, oh man. What a player.
I had that ready because you and I share that. I think he’s the tops. He just —

Absolutely. Absolutely. And you know back when I was — ’57, ’58, ’59 of course, when all those great Miles Davis Sextet albums were recorded I used to — I have told people, I’ve told kids when I teach to try to explain the difference between those three soloists: Miles Davis, John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley. You know Miles, and these are generalizations of course, but you know it’s more or less true, that Miles was very sophisticated and played — you know he held back a lot. He’d go [scats]. And you’d just wait for the note, what’s he going to do next? Actually you create a great deal of drama by doing that, you just draw people in by playing less. Then there’s Coltrane, who was on this search. They used to call it “sheets of sound.” But to me it sounded like he was on this incredible, unbelievable, fantastic search you know, and tons of notes and man it was like amazing. And then Cannonball comes on and he’s like, “Hey great day, isn’t it?” [scats] You know? Just happy. Just real happy. And it’s that attitude that I always related to because that was really me more than the other people, although as I say, I admired both Miles and Coltrane. I have all their records. And between those three people — Miles, Coltrane and Cannonball — those are the three biggest record, collections, parts of my record collection, those three.
And he was so effective as a band leader and a speaker. I mean he just was so hip, he’d stand up there and, I got to see him a number of times and I just was so sucked into him.

His vibe. Absolutely. Well he was a teacher in Florida as I understand. But what a player, what a marvelous player. I still, you know the one that kills me, it’s an album called “Nippon Soul.” And there’s a tune called “Easy to Love” the Cole Porter tune “Easy to Love.” He plays at a breakneck speed and he plays the most phenomenal solo that goes on and on, he never repeats himself. But it’s just, you can not believe the creativity and genius displayed in that solo. It’s unbelievable.

It’s like that recording of “Spectacular” — it’s like spectacular. But I always — we can get off this momentarily but it’s interesting that one of his biggest hits was of course “Mercy Mercy” which he does not solo on . I like to tell my students the greatest note ever played on the saxophone is when he goes [scats].
I got ya. That’s right. That’s exactly right. It just hits ya.
